If you ask five physicians a question, you might get eight different answers. Karan Singhal of @OpenAI on how OpenAI decides what its models should say about health:

"One of the first things that we did when we first started focusing on health at OpenAI was really build this kind of global physician network of hundreds of experts that we work with."

"Across the globe, across dozens of specialties and languages and countries of practice, to think about the right ways to aggregate the wisdom of experts so that we weren't relying, especially in areas where there could be disagreement, on one or two or three physicians to kind of adjudicate."

"Let's say the aggregated wisdom of the physicians is pointing in one direction, and then maybe the user actually wants you to say something comforting even when the situation's not comforting. There it's basically a prioritization of safety."

"It's very important to us that we take our obligation very seriously when there's hundreds of millions of health conversations coming in."

"We have evaluations that track these kind of difficult situations... Over time, we've not only improved how we've done that evaluation working with physicians, but also seen pretty dramatic model improvements across the board."

Karan Singhal of @OpenAI on why new clinical guidelines can take 5 to 17 years to reach everyday doctors, and why he wants to compress that to days or even hours:

"You basically have a bunch of people writing papers, biomedical papers of various kinds, suggesting improvements or treatments. And then you have this yearly process across different specialties of building clinical guidelines."

"These clinical guidelines are roughly, you can consider them kind of flowcharts... that describe roughly what you should do in different scenarios based on the latest research."

"So you have the biomedical literature, you have the clinical guidelines, and then you have what do people actually do in practice. The final step, it turns out, is a massive bottleneck."

"People have found that this takes, depending on the study, like 5 to 17 years for that penetration to actually happen. You don't wanna be practicing medicine 5 to 17 years behind."

"One of the things that we think about is how do you compress that kind of period of practicing in the past down to weeks or days or even hours."

@thekaransinghal @JayRughani

We believe solving dexterous manipulation is one of the largest opportunities in robotics. That’s why we're thrilled to lead Eka Robotics’ Series A.

Much of the world's physical economy still depends on people using their hands, and that work has been hard to automate because the real world is variable.

@EkaRobotics has built a Vision-Force-Action model that combines visual perception with force feedback from its robotic hands. The model, sensing, and hardware are designed together, so the robot can use physical contact itself as information.

If Eka’s approach works at scale, the implication is profound: robot experience can increasingly scale with compute rather than human labor.

Pulkit Agrawal is one of the leading researchers in robot learning and a pioneer in computational sensorimotor learning through work at his Improbable AI Lab at MIT CSAIL. Tuomas Haarnoja co-created a foundational algorithms in modern reinforcement learning at Berkeley and later worked at Google DeepMind training complex humanoid behaviors.

Congrats, @pulkitology, @haarnoja, and the Eka Robotics team!

By @stuffyokodraws and @RaghuRaghuram

US electricity prices are skyrocketing.

The average price of US residential electricity has risen +11% since January 2025, to 19.6 cents per kilowatt-hour in August 2026, near an all-time high.

Average prices during the first 8 months of 2026 were +40% higher than in the same period of 2019.

The largest increase in residential electricity prices over this period was in Maine, at +90%, followed by California and New York, at nearly +70%.

This comes as the AI boom is intensifying electricity demand, with data centers requiring enormous amounts of electricity to power thousands of chips and cooling systems. 

A 1-gigawatt data center can consume as much electricity as 800,000 homes.

As a result, wholesale electricity prices in areas near significant data center activity surged by as much as +267% between 2020 and 2025.

The AI revolution is driving a surge in electricity demand, and households are increasingly feeling the cost.
